title: Did leaving New Orleans change Louis's style?
summary: Perhonas's communal-versus-soloist theory, Louis becoming a soloist, and Giggy Williams calling the Hot Five novelty.

story.theme_name: Working with and around Louis Armstrong
story.community_name: Playing with and around Louis Armstrong

blocks.x: There's another, we were mentioning Louie just a minute ago. There is a notion that those early musicians who left New Orleans early, like King Oliver, Louie, that New Orleans was a very communal organization. The musicians stuck together and that was reflected in the style of music as well. And that those that left tended not to fit into the communal pattern of living. And that Louie might have been, you know, couldn't have played in an ensemble band or wasn't a communal soul.
We don't know what it's got. Kind of a rough kind of theory, but.

Probably Louie always was sensational in, soon after he started here and all, at least he, he probably, as far as his lip goes and a certain expressiveness there that was. But, so naturally he attracted attention and following and then he would try to please those people too. So when he got to Chicago and soon after that he became a more or less of a soloist. But, say, the Hot Fives, which have the small traditional group, you know, say five to seven players, but he still did a different style. I remember Giggy Williams, the guitar player in the original Creole band, when I first met him, also 1940 in Los Angeles. He lived down there near Zoo Robertson and near Bolden's sister-in-law and those people. And he was, started complaining about Louie Armstrong, said those are, those are novelty records. And he was thinking mostly of the Hot Five style.

Yeah, he called it, said that's novelty style. It wasn't, and yet they probably played at times that way here too. I imagine Louie probably, because people talk about, when they talk about like Cornet Chop Suey, they'll say, well, the first people, first person they ever heard play that. I think Lee Collins would say that was Buddy Petit used to play that almost note for note, like Cornet Chop Suey. Which is, largely features the trumpet, you know, not all the way through. But of course, even there they have a lot of solos, the trombone, or he was starting to take trombone solos. Even the Gut Bucket Blues, which they have that introduction, you know, on each number, each one plays a chorus and they make the announcement before.

Well, maybe the strict ensemble style, in a sense, or I don't know how you feel about this, kind of sold the seeds of its own destruction, like many styles do that have a, that are quite, they have a pretty formal pattern to them. And they're, they're quite strict in that, that they just don't last forever because of the, I mean, you know, I don't know.
There are some good ensembles, though, even in those early Louis things.
